sermon:
## The Old Commandment You Never Outgrew
*Walking in truth and love is not two things. It is one obedience with two names.*

**Text:** 2 John 1-6 · **Supporting:** John 13:34-35 · 1 John 2:7-8 · Deuteronomy 6:5-6 · 1 John 5:3

An old man writes a short letter to a church he calls a lady, and her members he calls her children, and he says he loves them. Then he tells us why. Not because they are warm. Not because they are growing. "Because of the truth that abides in us and will be with us forever" (2 John 2). The affection has a reason, and the reason is doctrinal, and somewhere in the modern church that sentence stopped making sense to us.

**Love That Knows the Difference Between Sentiment and Truth**
We have been taught that love is the soft thing and truth is the hard thing, and that a good pastor leads with the soft one. The elder will not let us keep the distinction. "The elder to the elect lady and her children, whom I love in truth, and not only I, but also all who know the truth, because of the truth that abides in us and will be with us forever" (2 John 1-2). Three times in one sentence, the truth. He does not say he loves them and also happens to believe true things. He says the love runs along the truth like a current along a wire. Take the wire away and the current has nowhere to go.

This is the same man who, in his first letter, refused to call the commandment new. "I am writing you no new commandment, but an old commandment that you had from the beginning" (1 John 2:7). And it is older than the beginning of the church. "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your might. And these words that I command you today shall be on your heart" (Deuteronomy 6:5-6). The command to love was never invented by the gentle. It was issued by God, in the desert, with weight. We did not soften it into a feeling. We were handed it as a law, and the law is that the truth and the love arrive together or not at all.

**Rejoicing Is a Verb You Can Watch**
Then the old man tells us what made him glad, and it is worth noticing how concrete it is. "I rejoiced greatly to find some of your children walking in the truth, just as we were commanded by the Father" (2 John 4). Not believing the truth in the abstract. Walking in it. He found people whose feet were going the direction their confession claimed. He did not rejoice that they had right opinions filed away somewhere. He rejoiced that you could follow them down a road and the road matched the words.

Notice the small ache buried in that verse. "Some of your children." Some. The historian in you wants to ask about the rest, and the pastor in him already has. A church is rarely all walking and never all wandering; it is usually some, and the some is enough to make a shepherd glad and not enough to let him stop praying. I have stood in my own pulpit and rejoiced over the some, and gone home and grieved over the rest, and called the rejoicing my ministry and the grieving my private burden, as if the two were not the same love wearing two faces. They are the same love. The man who only celebrates the some has stopped pastoring. The man who only grieves the rest has stopped believing the gospel can still move a foot.

Walking is the test the New Testament keeps coming back to because walking cannot be faked across a long enough distance. You can hold a true sentence for an hour. You cannot walk a true road for a decade without it becoming who you are. "And this is love, that we walk according to his commandments" (2 John 6). He has defined the word for us, and the definition has no exit. Love is not what you feel toward the commandments. Love is walking in them. The feeling may come and go. The walking is the thing.

**The Commandment We Keep Trying to Trade Up**
Hear the way he closes the loop, because it is doing more than it looks. "And now I ask you, dear lady, not as though I were writing you a new commandment, but the one we have had from the beginning, that we love one another" (2 John 5). He could have written something fresh. He is an apostle; the church would have received an innovation from his hand and built a conference around it. He refuses. The thing he presses on them is the thing they already had. From the beginning.

We are restless with the old commandment. We want the advanced version, the deeper teaching, the next thing past loving one another, because loving the people actually in front of us is the hardest assignment in the Christian life and we would rather graduate from it than fail at it. The elder will not let us graduate. He hands us back the first lesson and tells us it is also the last one. "For this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments. And his commandments are not burdensome" (1 John 5:3). Not new. Not advanced. Not the thing you outgrow on the way to maturity. The thing maturity finally learns to do.

And this is where the letter turns toward the One it has been about the whole time. The commandment we keep from the beginning is not a rule floating free of a face. It is the commandment of the One who walked it first and all the way down. "A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another: just as I have loved you, you also are to love one another" (John 13:34). The standard is not our affection. The standard is His cross. To abide in His teaching is to walk where He walked, in the truth, toward the people, at cost, and the love that does that is not something we generate. It is something we received, from the beginning, when He loved us first. The current runs from Him through the wire of His truth into the feet of a church that one old man was glad to find still walking.

Love is the old commandment, kept.

## The Door the Church Forgot It Was Allowed to Shut
*Some doors are hospitality. Some doors are surrender. The elder teaches us to tell them apart.*

**Text:** 2 John 7-13 · **Supporting:** 1 John 4:2-3 · 1 John 2:23 · Jude 3-4 · Romans 16:17

The gentlest letter in the New Testament ends by telling a church to leave a man standing on the porch. No meal. No greeting. The same elder who three times said he loved in the truth now says, of a certain kind of visitor, do not even tell him hello. We read it and flinch, because we have been catechized to believe the open door is the whole gospel. The elder believes the door has a hinge that swings both ways, and he is about to show us when it closes.

**The Lie Has an Address, and the Address Is the Body**
He names the danger with a precision we have lost the stomach for. "For many deceivers have gone out into the world, those who do not confess the coming of Jesus Christ in the flesh. Such a one is the deceiver and the antichrist" (2 John 7). Not deceivers in general. Not bad vibes. A specific lie with a specific shape: that Jesus Christ did not come in the flesh. The earliest heresy the church faced was not too little reverence for Jesus but too much of the wrong kind, a Christ too spiritual to bleed, too divine to have a body, too pure to touch the actual dirt of an actual death.

The elder had given the test already, and it is a strange test for how plain it is. "By this you know the Spirit of God: every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God, and every spirit that does not confess Jesus is not from God" (1 John 4:2-3). The flesh is the hinge of the whole thing. If Christ did not come in a body, He did not die in a body, and if He did not die in a body, there is no cross, and if there is no cross, there is no gospel, only a teacher, only an idea, only a feeling that asks nothing of your Tuesday. The deceiver does not usually arrive denying Jesus. He arrives admiring Jesus while quietly removing His body from the story. The denial is doctrinal, and the doctrine is the door.

**The Reward You Can Lose by Being Welcoming**
Then the warning turns and faces us, the welcomers, the ones who would never deny Christ ourselves but might host the man who does. "Watch yourselves, so that you may not lose what we have worked for, but may win a full reward" (2 John 8). Watch yourselves. Not watch them, yourselves. The danger to a faithful church is rarely that it suddenly stops believing. The danger is that it is too kind to notice when the deceiver moves in, and loses by hospitality what it would never have surrendered by argument.

He states the stakes without softening them. "Everyone who goes on ahead and does not abide in the teaching of Christ, does not have God. Whoever abides in the teaching has both the Father and the Son" (2 John 9). Goes on ahead. The deceiver is not behind the church, refusing to keep up. He is in front of it, the progressive, the advanced one, the man who has moved past the embarrassing particulars of the incarnation into something purer and higher. And the elder says the man who runs ahead of Christ has run out of God altogether. "No one who denies the Son has the Father. Whoever confesses the Son has the Father also" (1 John 2:23). You cannot keep the Father by trading away the Son. They come together or they go together. There is no version of the faith that holds onto God and lets go of the body of His Christ.

This is the verse Jude was contending for. "I found it necessary to write appealing to you to contend for the faith that was once for all delivered to the saints. For certain people have crept in unnoticed" (Jude 3-4). Crept in unnoticed. That is how it always happens. Not at the front door with a banner, but unnoticed, welcomed, fed, greeted, given the platform, because the church that prized its openness above its confession never learned to tell the guest from the wolf.

**The Door We Are Afraid to Close, and the One Who Earned It Shut**
Now the hard sentence, and I will not round its edges. "If anyone comes to you and does not bring this teaching, do not receive him into your house or give him any greeting, for whoever greets him takes part in his wicked works" (2 John 10-11). Paul said the same in his own way. "Watch out for those who cause divisions and create obstacles contrary to the doctrine that you have been taught; avoid them" (Romans 16:17). And we resist this, and we should examine why we resist it, because the resistance is not always righteous. Some of it is love. And some of it is cowardice wearing love's coat.

I have called my unwillingness to draw a line discernment when it was really fear of being thought unkind. I have left the door open not because I had thought carefully about hospitality but because closing it would cost me a reputation I was protecting. The elder is not licensing the suspicious, door-slamming spirit that hunts heretics for sport, that man has failed the first half of the letter, the love, the walking in truth. He is correcting the opposite failure, the one we are actually prone to: a church so terrified of being unwelcoming that it will host its own undoing and call the hosting grace.

Mark what the closed door is protecting. It is not the church's comfort. It is the church's reward, the full reward, the having of both the Father and the Son. The door is shut for the same reason the love was commanded, because the truth abides in us and we will not let it be carried off by a charming man with a hollow Christ. To abide in the teaching of Christ is to confess that He came in the flesh, that He died in that flesh, that He rose in it, and that the threshold of the church is finally His, not ours. The door belongs to the One who stood outside our own door first and was not received, who came in the flesh to the people who would not greet Him, and opened the only door that was ever shut against us by dying in the body the deceivers say He never had.

The elder ends almost lightly, ink running out, hoping to come and speak face to face, the children of your elect sister sending their greetings. A whole church, kept. A door, watched. A Christ, in the flesh, worth the trouble of telling some men no.

Some doors must stay shut.
